title: 2. Business Segments, Product Portfolio & Real-World Economics
book_title: Chapter 2: Inside the Molecule Factory — Segments, Customers & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: A single fluorine atom in the right position can turn a generic industrial intermediate into an irreplaceable solar or pharmaceutical reagent.
epigraph.author: Specialty Fluorochemicals Engineering Principle

web_blocks.html: In its audited Ind AS filings, Tanfac reports one main segment: "Fluorine-Based Chemicals / Specialty Chemicals" [1][5]. It does not publish a product-by-product revenue table [1][5]. Still, plant disclosures and industry data reveal a clear revenue split. Hydrofluoric Acid (HF) and its direct derivatives bring in roughly ~85% of sales, depending on cycle spreads [24]. Specialty Fluorides and allied inorganic chemicals add the other ~15% [24]. Every product starts from one integrated chemical tree at Cuddalore. Imported acid-grade fluorspar (CaF2) reacts with captive sulphuric acid (H2SO4) in rotary kilns to form Anhydrous Hydrofluoric Acid (AHF) [2][3][8]. From there, the acid branches into merchant AHF, ultra-pure solar-grade DHF, Aluminium Fluoride, potassium salts, and new fluorocarbons [2][3][8].

web_blocks.html: 1. Anhydrous Hydrofluoric Acid (AHF) & Diluted HF (29,700 MTPA): Picture a mid-sized Indian agrochemical or drug intermediate maker producing fluorinated herbicides or API building blocks. They cannot buy HF on spot exchanges or store it in plain steel drums. AHF boils at 19.5°C, burns human tissue on contact, and eats through glass. Buyers order bulk AHF directly from Tanfac in lined road tankers or T14 ISO tanks [2][26]. At Cuddalore, Tanfac reacts imported acid-spar with captive sulphuric acid in hot kilns [4][15]. It scrubs and distills the gas to >99.9% purity, then bills on formula-linked B2B contracts tied to landed fluorspar and sulphur prices [4][15]. Capacity doubled to 29,700 MTPA in October 2024, giving AHF both merchant sales and captive feed for every downstream line [11].

2. Solar-Grade Dilute Hydrofluoric Acid (10,000 TPA, AHF basis): Indian solar PV makers scaling TOPCon or heterojunction (HJT) cell lines face a strict hurdle [3][12]. Every silicon wafer needs wet-chemical etching and oxide removal using ultra-pure Dilute HF [3][12]. Metallic impurities in that acid must stay in parts per billion (ppb) [3][12]. Until recently, Indian solar cell makers imported this grade at high freight cost and delivery risk. Tanfac started Phase 1 (5,000 TPA) in June 2025 and Phase 2 (5,000 TPA) in October 2025 [3][12]. It became India's first local maker of Solar-Grade DHF [3][12]. By purifying its own AHF through multi-stage distillation and clean packaging, Tanfac wins a local import-replacement niche with much stickier client ties than basic acid [4][12].

3. Aluminium Fluoride (~15,600–16,500 MTPA): A primary aluminium smelter running high-current Hall-Héroult pots needs Aluminium Fluoride (AlF3) non-stop [2][15]. It lowers the melting point of the cryolite-alumina bath and keeps electric current flowing smoothly [2][15]. Tanfac reacts HF with alumina hydrate to make dry, free-flowing AlF3 powder [2]. Yet global smelters buy AlF3 through tight annual tenders pegged to Chinese export rates [15][16]. As a result, this legacy line carries thinner spreads and sharp price cycles [15][16].

4. Specialty Fluorides & Organics (KF, KHF2, BF3 Complexes, IBAP — 8,400+ MTPA): An API plant making ibuprofen needs Isobutyl Acetophenone (IBAP) [2][4][24]. Meanwhile, a fluorination plant—including co-promoter Anupam Rasayan—needs dry Potassium Fluoride (KF) as a halogen-exchange agent [2][4][24]. Tanfac makes KF and Potassium Bifluoride (KHF2) by mixing HF with potassium hydroxide, then drying and sizing the salt to strict moisture limits [2][24]. It also sells Boron Trifluoride (BF3) complexes and sodium silico-fluoride [2][24]. These specialty salts earn higher prices per tonne than bulk AlF3. They also deepen Tanfac's share across farm, heavy-water, brazing, and drug supply chains [24].

5. Captive Sulphuric Acid & Oleum (~100,000 MTPA) and Future R-32 / Japanese Contract (20,000 MTPA): Tanfac burns imported molten or granular sulphur in its captive contact plant at Cuddalore [2][24]. This makes sulphuric acid and oleum to feed its HF kilns, while surplus acid goes to local buyers [2][24]. Looking to January 2027, Tanfac is building a ₹495 crore, 20,000 MTPA downstream plant for HFC-32 refrigerant gas and specialty fluorinated intermediates [8][9]. Already, 7,500 MTPA (37.5% of capacity) is locked into a 7-year Japanese supply deal worth ₹337.5 crore per year (₹2,362.5 crore total ex-GST) [8][9]. That deal turns raw HF capacity into steady, multi-year export sales.

To see why downstream upgrading lifts unit returns, follow the value chain per tonne of fluorine atom. In legacy Aluminium Fluoride (AlF3), Tanfac reacts HF with alumina hydrate for smelters [2][15][16]. Prices track global benchmarks where Chinese excess supply often caps spreads [2][15][16]. In Potassium Fluoride (KF) and Potassium Bifluoride (KHF2), mixing HF with potassium hydroxide yields high-purity reagents [2][24]. Farm active makers, drug plants, heavy-water units, and brazing shops pay much more per tonne of HF consumed [2][24]. Likewise, Isobutyl Acetophenone (IBAP) links Tanfac straight into painkiller API chains like ibuprofen [2][24].

In Solar-Grade DHF (10,000 TPA), the moat shifts from reaction chemistry to trace cleaning [3][12]. Silicon wafer fabs running TOPCon and HJT lines need etching acids free of metal ions that hurt cell output [12]. Client testing takes months of batch checks and clean-pack audits [4][12]. Once a domestic solar maker approves Tanfac's Cuddalore stream, switching costs rise sharply [4][12]. Next, the 20,000 MTPA R-32 / fluorinated chemicals plant moves Tanfac into organic fluorocarbons [4][8][9]. Pairing captive AHF with chlorinated inputs serves HFC-32 cooling demand under Kigali rules, while locking 7,500 MTPA into the 7-year Japanese export deal [4][8][9].

Customer Concentration, Qualification Cycles & Pricing Formulas: Across its ₹711 crore FY2026 sales base, Tanfac serves over 100 industrial clients [10]. Still, client loyalty varies widely by line. In legacy Aluminium Fluoride (AlF3), smelters run annual or half-year tenders tied to landed Chinese quotes, leaving low switching costs [15][16]. In Anhydrous HF, buyers in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, and Gujarat rely on Tanfac's tanker fleet for just-in-time supply [26]. Storing bulk toxic liquid HF on-site brings steep safety and insurance costs [26]. In Solar-Grade DHF and the Japanese chemical stream, testing takes months of trace-impurity checks, building multi-year lock-in [4][9][12].

By-Product & Co-Product Synergy: Inside an integrated HF site, waste handling and co-products shape unit margins [2][18]. Reacting fluorspar with sulphuric acid leaves calcium sulphate (anhydrite/gypsum) as a solid by-product alongside HF gas [2]. Managing gypsum disposal, scrubbing tail gases, and reusing heat from the ~100,000 MTPA sulphuric acid plant cuts net cost per tonne of AHF [2][24]. Meanwhile, Boron Trifluoride (BF3) complexes and Potassium Bifluoride (KHF2) earn higher revenue per fluorine atom [2][24]. Tanfac serves small-batch drug, nuclear/heavy-water, and brazing clients without adding heavy kiln tonnage [2][24].

book_paragraphs: Step onto the Cuddalore plant floor and one truth stands out: Tanfac does not sell finished consumer goods. It sells reactivity. In its Ind AS accounts, the company reports one umbrella line: Fluorine-Based Chemicals. Yet inside that single line sits a layered chemical tree. Roughly 85% of revenue comes from Hydrofluoric Acid and its direct offshoots, while about 15% comes from specialty fluorides.

To see why this setup matters, follow how one molecule feeds the next. At the base, Tanfac burns sulphur to make up to 100,000 tonnes a year of captive sulphuric acid. It feeds that acid and imported fluorspar into rotary kilns to make Anhydrous Hydrofluoric Acid, or AHF. In October 2024, Tanfac doubled that AHF base from 14,850 to 29,700 tonnes per year. Every other product is simply a downstream choice for where to send that AHF.

The brightest downstream move so far is Solar-Grade Dilute Hydrofluoric Acid. Picture an Indian solar cell maker running TOPCon or heterojunction wafer lines. Before a silicon wafer becomes a solar cell, its surface needs etching with dilute HF so pure that trace metals stay in parts per billion. Until 2025, Indian solar plants imported that pure acid at steep freight cost. By starting 5,000 tonnes of Solar DHF in June 2025 and 5,000 tonnes in October 2025, Tanfac became India's first local maker. It turned a basic acid into a sticky import-replacement reagent.

Compare that with Tanfac's old workhorse, Aluminium Fluoride. Primary aluminium smelters need AlF3 to lower the melting point of their reduction pots. Tanfac holds roughly 15,600 to 16,500 tonnes of capacity here, reacting HF with alumina hydrate. It brings steady volume, yet smelters buy through tight tenders against Chinese imports, capping pricing power. That is why Tanfac's 8,400-plus tonnes of specialty fluorides matter far more for margin quality. This group spans Potassium Fluoride, Potassium Bifluoride, Boron Trifluoride complexes, and IBAP used in ibuprofen.

Think of a farm chemical chemist building a fluorinated active ingredient. They need dry Potassium Fluoride for halogen exchange and cannot risk moisture in the salt. Tanfac reacts its own HF with potassium hydroxide, sizes the salt to tight specs, and ships it to drug and farm plants, including co-promoter Anupam Rasayan.

Now comes the biggest downstream bet yet: a ₹495 crore, 20,000-tonne fluorinated chemicals and R-32 gas plant approved in January 2026. Unlike open-market bets, 7,500 tonnes—roughly 37.5% of the plant—is already pre-sold. A 7-year Japanese supply deal starting January 2027 locks in ₹337.5 crore of annual sales. If built on time, Tanfac shifts from a regional acid vendor to a contracted global supplier.

Why does upgrading a single fluorine molecule matter so much? Think of the gap between selling plain flour and selling drug-grade excipients. When Tanfac turns HF into Aluminium Fluoride for smelters, it competes on tender price against global commodity rivals. When it turns that same HF into Solar-Grade DHF, metal traces must drop to parts per billion so they do not ruin TOPCon solar cells. Once a solar fab approves your acid, it rarely switches just to save a few rupees per kilo.

The same rule holds for Potassium Fluoride, Potassium Bifluoride, Boron Trifluoride complexes, and IBAP. Each downstream step adds tighter moisture control, custom sizing, or extra distillation. Each step moves Tanfac away from commodity tenders toward spec-driven B2B contracts. The 20,000-tonne R-32 and fluorinated chemicals plant climbs one rung higher into organic fluorocarbons and contracted Japanese supply.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The real story at Tanfac is value per fluorine atom. Selling raw AlF3 on smelter tenders is a spread-defense game. Upgrading that same AHF molecule into parts-per-billion Solar DHF or a 7-year Japanese chemical deal changes both client lock-in and switching costs.

book_subsections.title: Why Single-Segment Reporting Hides the Mix Shift
paragraphs: Tanfac reports only one segment in its annual report. You will not find a neat table comparing Solar DHF margins against Aluminium Fluoride margins in the notes. That gap hides pricing data from rivals, yet forces us to watch physical plant ramp-ups, working capital turns, and blended EBITDA margins to see if the specialty mix is lifting profits.
In practice, when Aluminium Fluoride tenders tighten or merchant AHF spreads cool—as in FY2026—only fast volume growth in Solar DHF and potassium salts can defend blended margins.

book_subsections.title: The Captive Sulphuric Acid Advantage
paragraphs: Running an 82,500-to-100,000-tonne sulphuric acid plant inside the same Cuddalore fence helps unit costs in two quiet ways. It removes outside acid transport risk for the HF kilns, and its reaction heat makes process steam that cuts site power bills.

book_subsections.title: Product-Mix Economics: Spreads vs. Qualification Moats
paragraphs: Across Tanfac's lineup, products sit on a clear moat ladder. At the commodity base sit merchant sulphuric acid and Aluminium Fluoride, where spreads swing with global tenders. In the middle sits merchant AHF, shielded locally by hazardous-trucking friction. At the top sit Solar-Grade DHF, custom potassium salts, and the Japanese chemical stream, where long client audits and multi-year deals anchor plant use.

book_subsections.title: The Hidden Economics of Just-in-Time Hazardous Delivery
paragraphs: Why does a drug intermediate plant in Hyderabad or Ankleshwar buy Anhydrous HF from Cuddalore instead of importing drums? Nobody wants fifty tonnes of fuming, boiling hydrogen fluoride sitting in their own yard for three months. By running a fleet of lined road tankers and ISO tanks, Tanfac acts as its clients' just-in-time chemical warehouse. It absorbs the storage and safety burden at Cuddalore so buyers can run lean stocks.

That setup also shows why utility integration inside Cuddalore matters so much. Burning sulphur in the captive acid plant makes process steam that lowers energy bills. Meanwhile, scrubbing tail gases and handling calcium sulphate gypsum keeps TNPCB compliance clean. Every rupee saved on utilities or acid freight flows straight into conversion costs, helping Tanfac stay competitive when fluorspar prices swing.
